Opening

2

Where we are in the semester

Topic 2 of 13, week 2 of 14 – the week that builds the vocabulary. Today: what a pattern is, the four families, the living references, and when you may break a pattern; three activities, AI excluded. Exercise U1 comes right after this topic: one app, its claims (Topic 1) and its patterns (today). Pattern analysis is learning objective 3 · Bloom 3 in the naming, 5 in the verdicts. What you should already know is in the script: a pattern is a named, recurring solution to a recurring design problem, proven by use. The term comes from architecture (Christopher Alexander, A Pattern Language, 1977) and entered software via object-oriented design before UX adopted it. Distinguish three things models and juniors reliably conflate: the pattern (the reusable idea: "persistent bottom-level navigation with 3–5 top destinations"), the component (one platform's implementation: UITabBar), and the guideline (one platform's rules for using it: the HIG chapter). A pattern language is the connected vocabulary that lets teams argue about design without pointing and grunting. That is the sense we use all semester.

3 principle

Patterns are congealed experience – and precisely therefore potentially outdated the moment you need them.

A pattern earns its authority from the past: thousands of apps, millions of interactions, slowly grinding a solution smooth. That grinding takes years, so every catalog describes the apps of the years before it went to print. In most engineering disciplines this lag is harmless; a bridge truss from 1990 still holds. Interfaces are different. Their ground truth is user expectation, and expectation moves with every platform release.

4 question

Who caught themselves this week operating an app without looking? quick round · two prepared moments to start

The thumb finds the tab bar of Monzo while the eyes read the feed (card 6). The swipe back on iOS replaced a button nobody aims at any more (clip in the appendix).

5 definition

Pattern

A named, recurring solution to a recurring design problem – proven by use, not by argument.

  • The name lets a team argue about a screen without pointing and grunting: that is what named buys
  • Recurring means problem and solution return across thousands of apps; a trick used in a single app gets no name
  • Millions of operations ground the solution smooth, without a committee or a standard behind it: proven by use
  • That separates patterns from style guides, which justify their rules on paper, and from taste
  • Expectation conformity has become muscle memory: the thumb knows where the tab bar lives because a thousand apps agreed to put it there
6

What a pattern is not

Pattern, component and guideline are three different things, and models and juniors reliably mix them up.

  • A pattern is no law: you may break it if you know what you pay (later today)
  • UITabBar is one platform's component, an implementation of the idea
  • The HIG chapter is a guideline: one platform's rules for using the idea
  • "It's the standard" has never saved a bad form, so it works as no excuse either
7 principle

Put a tab bar in your app and you borrow the expectation a thousand other apps already taught your users.

Seen from the user's side, other people's apps have already taught where the back button sits and what a pull on a list does. An app that uses the pattern starts with that trust. An app that breaks it asks its users to relearn, and the second half of today is about what that costs.

The four families

8

Family 1 · Navigation Where am I, where can I go, how do I get back?

Each navigation pattern answers the three questions differently, and the choice says what your app considers important.

  • The tab bar shows everything and carries at most five destinations, always visible and paid for in screen space
  • A navigation drawer hides and scales: room for twenty entries, at the price that nobody sees them
  • Hub & spoke forces every route through the center. Clean separation, slow switching.
  • One step at a time, one way through: sequential flow is the shape of checkout and onboarding
9

Family 2 · Forms Every field is a question. Every question costs.

In forms, patterns turn into money most directly: each extra field is one more question before the goal.

  • With inline validation the form checks each field while you type, and the error appears where it happens
  • The number field opens the number pad. A full keyboard under a phone-number field breaks the promise of input-appropriate keyboards.
  • Progressive disclosure: ask later what you do not need now. The shipping address can wait until something ships.
  • What extra steps cost in a real case is measured in Topic 7
10

Family 3 · Feedback The system speaks: status, progress, success, failure.

Feedback patterns run the conversation between system and user.

  • Optimistic UI acts as if it worked and repairs if it did not: the message shows as sent before the server confirms
  • Skeleton screens show the shape of what is coming. A gray placeholder feels faster than a spinner over nothing.
  • Act first, offer reversal, and skip the nagging "Are you sure?" beforehand: undo over confirm
  • The quietly radical member is undo-over-confirm, faster and more respectful, but only where reversal is actually possible. Keep that precondition for Topic 9.
  • Error messages use plain language, name the problem precisely and suggest a way out, visible on the screen rather than in a modal
11

Family 4 · Search The family everyone forgets until the app grows.

The pattern that matters most is the least glamorous one: what the app does at zero results.

  • Type-ahead suggests while the user is still typing, because steering a query beats repairing one
  • Search where the user already stands before searching everything and finding too much: scoped search
  • An empty list is a dead end; a good zero-state is a switch. Zero-results recovery loosens the filter, fixes the typo, offers the neighbor category.
  • Search gets designed last because on day one there is nothing to find. By the time there is, the budget is gone.

Activity 1 · Name the pattern

12 exercise

Name the pattern Activity 1 · 16 minutes

Task: Each group gets three screenshot cards. Per card: which pattern, which family – recognized by what?

Time: 10 minutes work + 6 minutes resolution · Form: teams of three or four, results on the cards

Result: three identifications, each with its recognition feature

AI role: excluded. The vocabulary must live in your head – today your own eye is the tool under test.

13

The twelve cards

Twelve screenshot cards of real apps, taken from this course's 2025 slide sets; eleven were curated by Mobbin.

  • Three cards per group, distributed at random
  • Every family appears at least twice: navigation, forms, feedback, search
  • Two of the twelve are contestable: they fit two families
  • The source of every card is on record: app, 2025 slide set and page
  • The deliverable is the recognition feature, for example "position, persistence, icon-text pairing"
14

Name the pattern – 10 minutes

Which pattern, which family – recognized by what?

  • Three cards per team of three or four
  • Per card one line: pattern · family · "I recognize it by …"
  • Results on the cards; all groups report afterwards
  • AI role: excluded
15

Resolution: all identifications

The identifications are collected at the front – the contestable cards come last.

  • All groups report: pattern, family, recognition feature
  • For the two contestable cards, both assignments are defensible
  • What decides is which user problem you consider primary, and that choice belongs to the design
16

The two contestable cards search, filter, or navigation?

The living references

17

The bookshelf, honestly

Both printed pattern books still teach structure, and their screenshots show the apps of 2014 and 2020.

  • In Tidwell et al., Designing Interfaces (3rd ed., 2020), the taxonomy still stands as the best printed structure we have
  • Its screenshots are historical documents
  • Neil, Mobile Design Pattern Gallery (2014) was long this module's compulsory reading
  • No successor volume exists (verified Aug 2026); her gallery lives on as a website
18

Mobbin updated weekly – the de-facto successor of every printed pattern gallery

  • Shipping products, screenshot by screenshot, searchable by pattern: real apps from the stores
  • With weekly updates the reference moves at the speed of the app stores, which no book can
  • What it proves is convergence: how many current apps solve one problem the same way
  • Live demo now: one pattern, empty state, across twenty current apps

Source: mobbin.com

19

The two platform contracts – both rebuilt in 2025

Apple · HIG, Liquid Glass (June 2025)

  • The platform's own promise, redesigned for iOS 26
  • The reference behind millions of apps moved underneath them

Google · Material 3 Expressive (May 2025)

  • Announced at I/O, rolled out through Wear OS (Aug 2025)
  • Same movement, same year: competition for expressiveness after a decade of flat design

Whoever learned patterns from a book in 2025 learned a dialect the platforms were already leaving. Describing what changed still takes the old vocabulary.

20 principle

What you look up in the HIG today can read differently by the colloquium.

Read the three sources as three kinds of evidence: Mobbin shows convergence (what everyone does), the HIG and Material state intent (what the platform promises), and Tidwell supplies structure (how to think about both). None of them is neutral. Mobbin, the HIG and Material all moved within the last eighteen months; only Tidwell stands still in its 2020 edition. What you look up today can look different by the end of the semester.

Activity 2 · Concept test

21 exercise

One concept test, peer-instruction style Activity 2 · 8 minutes

Task: Vote alone → two minutes with your neighbor → vote again.

Time: 8 minutes · Form: solo, then pairs

Result: two votes – show of hands or Moodle poll

AI role: excluded. The first vote only teaches if it is yours.

22

Concept test · Pull-to-refresh in a settings list: pattern correctly applied?

  1. Yes – consistency wins
  2. No – wrong context
  3. Harmless either way
23

Resolution: B – the pattern promises new content from outside

Settings do not change from outside – here the promise cannot be kept.

  • Pull-to-refresh promises new content arriving from elsewhere: the feed, the inbox
  • Whoever said A: consistency is a means to met expectations. Applied here, it produces a false one.
  • In the wrong place, the pattern teaches users a false expectation
  • Whoever said C: exactly this presumption of harmlessness goes on trial in the next half hour

Why patterns break

24 principle

Drop the text labels from a tab bar and you have claimed your users already know the icons.

Whoever breaks implicitly claims: my users do not need the promise – or my new promise is stronger. That claim can be tested with users, and case 1 later today is exactly this one.

25

Three legitimate reasons to break and no fourth

Every legitimate break points to something that changed: the device, the gesture, or the message.

  • Smartwatch navigation could not inherit the tab bar: a new device class where the pattern never fit
  • System-wide swipe gestures demoted the back button, so a new gesture or capability can make a pattern obsolete
  • The rarest and riskiest reason is deliberate contrast: the break is the message
26

27 principle

The fourth reason is that nobody thought about it, and from outside it can look exactly like courage.

Watch this one most closely. The procedure that follows asks for the price, and whoever broke a pattern without thinking cannot name it.

28

Case: Liquid Glass breaks Apple's own rules

June 2025: Apple's new design language contradicts conventions Apple itself set in 2024. Innovation – or fashion cycle?

  • Our position, offered for friction: two-thirds fashion cycle, one-third genuine evolution
  • The counterargument has weight. Whoever never breaks turns to stone; Flat Design was a break in 2013 too, and became a decade's norm.
  • Here the platform breaks its own promise, set only a year earlier

The trial

29 exercise

Verdict with a price Activity 3 · 18 minutes

Task: Three prepared pattern breaks are on trial. Per break, your group decides: innovation or error? Mandatory part: what does your verdict cost?

Time: 10 minutes work + 5 minutes resolution · Form: teams of three or four, one verdict card per case

Result: verdict + named price, per case – a verdict without a price is not counted

AI role: excluded. The judgment is the skill under training – there is no master solution to look up.

30

The verdict card

31

The three cases

Three prepared breaks, each drawn from Mobbin with its source line.

  • Three breaks, handed out as screenshot cards (cases 1–3 in the appendix)
  • Case 1: a tab bar without text labels
  • Case 2: a tab bar whose middle tab is a primary action, once stamped an anti-pattern
  • Case 3: a warning with only one button
  • Selection criterion: the case must carry an argument on both sides
  • Your own finds argue better, because their finders are in the room: bring them to Exercise U1, where the deviation field asks for exactly this
32

Verdict with a price – 10 minutes

Per case: innovation or error – and what does your verdict cost?

  • One verdict card per case: case · verdict · price, one sentence each
  • "Innovation" costs the learning effort of every user arriving with the old expectation
  • "Error" possibly costs a better solution the catalog cannot yet see
  • Stuck? Name the reason behind the break: one of the three legitimate reasons (device, gesture, message), or nobody thought about it
  • AI role: excluded
33

Resolution: the verdicts

Verdict cards side by side – we discuss only where groups diverge.

  • Where all groups agree, we move on and give the time to divergence
  • To both sides: which price was named, and which one concealed?
  • We document the dispute and leave it open
34

What we keep from the fight

Disagreement with named prices

  • is a design review
  • both sides leave with a sharper design

Disagreement without prices

  • is a taste battle
  • nobody learns anything; someone merely wins

Judge a break by the price someone can name for it.

The procedure comes back three times. Topic 3 asks which broken promise actually hurts. In Topic 6 you meet machines that break patterns without knowing them, a different error type. Topic 10 brings breaks designed to harm users. And in Topic 13 all thirteen conflict sentences get sorted, this one among them.

What counts for the exam today

Exam-relevant (LO 3) – this is the analysis grid of your seminar-paper analysis chapter.

  • The four families and their core patterns, with recognition features; pattern vs. component vs. guideline
  • What each living reference is evidence of: convergence (Mobbin) · intent (HIG, Material) · structure (Tidwell)
  • The three legitimate break reasons, and the illegitimate one
  • Verdict-with-price as the judgment procedure: innovation or error, and what the verdict costs
  • Question pool, from today: "Screenshot – name pattern and family, and what breaks if you swap it?"
  • Question pool, verbatim: "Here is a pattern break. Innovation or error? Name the price of your verdict."
37 question

What we did not settle today When breaking a pattern is brilliance and when it is negligence

Today gave us a judgment procedure, and no formula. Our verdicts bind nobody: the market reruns this trial every day, with N in the millions, and it is allowed to disagree with us.

Concept test 1 · Bottom navigation or tab bar – and is that the same thing?

  1. Same thing
  2. Different patterns, same family
  3. Different families
46

Resolution: B – different patterns, same family

Android and iOS terminology split what is functionally almost the same thing.

  • Functionally, A is right, yet the names carry each platform's rules with them
  • B is the most defensible answer: two named patterns, one family, one job
  • Whoever picks C confuses implementation and idea; the component is not the pattern

48

Where the pattern language comes from

A Pattern Language (1977) collected solutions that builders had used long before Alexander gave them names. UX catalogs work the same way: they name what many apps already do, so a catalog is as current as the apps it looked at.

49

The card set for printing twelve cards, answer key in the note of the card slide

50 definition

Affordance

Affordance is the quality of an object that lets users know which actions can be performed.

  • Real life: door knobs and drawer handles show where to grip
  • Software: drag handles, page peels, controls that look pressable
  • Touch adds gestures, most commonly tap, swipe or flick, and drag, and with them more possible affordances
  • Flat design made tappable elements harder to recognize; it can still provide affordance, but it takes more design skill
  • Many gestures show no affordance at all: users have to discover them, and may not be willing to learn app-specific tricks
51

Sparring check for self-study, copy-ready

Check question: Ask the model to describe Apple's current design language and when the HIG last changed fundamentally. If it describes pre-2025 conventions without mentioning Liquid Glass and iOS 26, it is answering from a world that no longer exists – the corrective is section 3 of the script.

Warning: Models trained before mid-2025 confidently describe the old design languages as current, invent pattern names that appear in no catalog, and cite Tidwell for claims the book does not make.

52

Sparring partner block for the exercise sheet, copy-ready

Deepening prompt 1 (refutation): "Refute as strongly as you can: 'A designer who cannot name the price of breaking a pattern should not break it.' Find real cases where great mobile design emerged from breaks nobody could have priced in advance."

Deepening prompt 2 (dissection sparring): "I am dissecting [app] along four pattern families (navigation, forms, feedback, search). Here is my naming for the navigation family: [paste]. Challenge it: offer the strongest alternative naming, and tell me which recognition feature would decide between us."

Warning: Pattern names you plan to use in your seminar paper need a locatable source – Tidwell chapter, HIG section, or Mobbin category, with the access date. Models invent pattern names that appear in no catalog.

53

To think further

  • If patterns are named too late by construction, what is the epistemically honest way to design in the gap between a platform shift and its new catalog?
  • Does Mobbin's convergence evidence cause the convergence it documents, and is that a problem, or just how languages work?
  • When Apple breaks Apple's rules, whose promise was broken, and who pays?
  • Which pattern do you personally follow purely because questioning it never occurred to you, and what would checking cost?
